newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Diplomats see tougher action against war criminals.
newsitem.headline: Diplomats see tougher action against war criminals.

text.p: NATO's swoop to grab two Serb indicted war criminals on Thursday reflected an international decision to get tougher with obstacles to a lasting peace in Bosnia, Western diplomats said on Thursday.

But NATO insisted the action, in which one indictee was shot dead while resisting arrest and the other captured, did not signal a shift in its policy to seize suspects only when encountered in the course of their peacekeeping patrols.

Simo Drljaca, the former Serb police chief of Prijedor, was killed on Thursday after firing on NATO soldiers trying to arrest him for war crimes. Milan Kovacevic, director of Prijedor hospital, was apprehended in the same operation.
Both were under so-called sealed indictments for complicity in genocide issued by the International Criminal Tribunal on former Yugoslavia (ICTY), based in The Hague.
In a statement, NATO said the action by its peace Stabilisation Force (SFOR) troops was fully in keeping with its mandate to detain indicted war criminals "when encountered".
The alliance has long argued against taking on the risky role of policeman in Bosnia and actively hunt down indictees who have circulated freely since the end of the war in 1995.

But diplomats said Thursday's move reflected growing frustration in Western capitals at the continuing presence of accused war criminals in Bosnia who retain major influence in politics and block reconciliation of Serbs, Moslems and Croats.

They noted at recent meetings -- of NATO ministers in Sintra, Portugal and government chiefs at this week's summit in Madrid -- that NATO governments had sent stronger messages than before about the need to bring in dozens of indictees at large.
These messages were directed, they said, at SFOR commanders on the ground in Bosnia who have considerable leeway in how aggressively they seek out "encounters" with war-crimes suspects.
"Madrid showed the political will is there," one Western diplomatic source said.

He said Thursday's action in the Prijedor area, the scene of notorious Serb prison camps for Moslems and Croats during the war and still a hotbed of Serb ultra-nationalism, was "an obvious sign of increased vigour by the international community."

Diplomats noted that aside from the Prijedor episode, the former rebel Serb mayor of Vukovar in nearby Croatia was arrested last month by U.N. soldiers carrying out a sealed indictment and jailed in The Hague to await trial.

Even the European Union was ratcheting up pressure, they noted. The European Commission has announced a freeze on aid to the Serb republic entity in Bosnia until former president and indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic is arrested.
NATO leaders are particularly concerned at the moment about an apparent power play against current Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic by hardliners loyal to Karadzic.

One diplomat said there was deep concern in capitals supplying SFOR troops that unless Karadzic and other high profile indictees are brought to book, it will be difficult to achieve a withdrawal from a peaceful and reconstructed Bosnia.
